subject_line: Aleya and the abandoned book in The Lightning of Possible Storms
email_body:
Dear Jonathan,

The frame of The Lightning of Possible Storms caught my attention: Aleya, a café server, finding a book its author has left behind, and the stories spilling out from there. Reviewers have argued over whether it is really a collection at all, and it went on to win the 2021 Margaret Laurence Award for Fiction.

I would love to ask how you think about the line between a story collection and a single strange machine.

subject_line: Edmonton's courtrooms in The Apocalypse of Morgan Turner
email_body:
Dear Jennifer,

The Apocalypse of Morgan Turner sets a young woman in contemporary Edmonton against the slow machinery of a trial for her sister's killer, and I was struck that you chose your own city, rather than somewhere invented, as the ground for that story. It reads as a sharp turn after Love Letters of the Angels of Death and Sistering.

I would be glad to ask how Edmonton shaped the book, and how a trial changes the way a family tells its grief.

book_title: Skating Wild on an Inland Sea
subject_line: Wild ice and an inland sea, from Thunder Bay
email_body:
Dear Jean,

The title Skating Wild on an Inland Sea stayed with me: the idea of a lake large enough to be called a sea, and a moment when it turns into a surface you can glide across. Coming from a writer based in Thunder Bay, it seems drawn from a very particular stretch of shoreline and winter.

I would love to ask how that place found its way into the book.

subject_line: From the stage to Kylie's magicians' showcase
email_body:
Dear Marty,

I have been reading about Kylie the Magnificent, the 14-year-old chasing a place in a magicians' showcase with her friend Min, alongside Willpower and Jennifer Mah's telekinetic rescue mission. What interests me is the line running back from these Orca middle-grade books to a stage play like Mom, Dad - I'm Living with a White Girl.

I would love to ask what the theatre taught you about writing for young readers.

subject_line: Sál, the escaped elephant, and a 600-year-old narrator
email_body:
Dear Thomas,

Handing the narration of The Elephant on Karlův Bridge to the Charles Bridge itself, six centuries old and watching Sál wander out of the Prague Zoo, is such a sure-footed choice. Kerry Clare called the book an absorbing literary puzzle, and I can see why.

I would love to ask how you found the bridge's voice, and what drew a writer launching books at Audrey's in Edmonton so deeply into Prague.

subject_line: A dancer, an avalanche, and the lodge in The Retreat
email_body:
Dear Elisabeth,

The Retreat puts a former dancer in a remote Rocky Mountain arts lodge, hoping to build a dance company, and then lets an avalanche cut the place off just as the filmmaker Anna Barthelmy is found dead in the snow. Turning a residency into a sealed room is a sharp idea.

I would love to ask what an arts retreat offered you as a setting for suspense, and how a dancer's sense of the body shaped the way you wrote fear.

subject_line: Marsali, Muckleton and the gun in Monet's window
email_body:
Dear Carmel,

In Field of Poppies, Marsali's close reading of Monet's poppies at Argenteuil turns up something unsettling, the possibility of a gun pointing from a window of the lovely house in the background. That detail seems to hold the whole Muckleton story in small: a country idyll, Alice Dooley's disappearance, a planned mine, and a couple finally retreating to a Melbourne high-rise.

I would love to ask where that reading of the painting began, and what drew you to the dream of the rural house.

book_title: The Wondrous Tale of Lavender Wolfe
subject_line: A kitchen rat called Hans Whitby, aboard a cursed ship
email_body:
Dear Karen,

In The Wondrous Tale of Lavender Wolfe, a small thief is snatched onto a cursed pirate ship in 1719, renamed Hans Whitby and set to work as a kitchen rat. That renaming feels like the heart of it: a child forced to become someone else just to survive the voyage.

I would love to ask how you found your way to 1719 and the sea, and whether your years working as a nurse still shape how you write children in danger.

book_title: The Bee and the Orange Tree
subject_line: The woman behind the first fairy tale
email_body:
Dear Melissa,

The framing of your Late Night Live conversation with Phillip Adams, "the woman behind the first fairy tale", stayed with me after reading about The Bee and the Orange Tree. Building a novel around a figure who stands at the origin of a whole genre, yet is rarely named, is a quietly bold choice.

I would be glad to ask how you research a life like that, and where history stops and the fairy tale takes over.

subject_line: Clio, horses and Bronze Age Crete in Cuckoo's Flight
email_body:
Dear Wendy,

Cuckoo's Flight closes a striking trio with Dragonfly Song and Swallow's Dance, and I was drawn to Clio, a fourteen-year-old who has to rethink her whole relationship with horses after a riding accident. Returning three times to Bronze Age Crete, each time through a different girl, is an unusual commitment for a children's writer.

I would love to ask what keeps pulling you back to that island.

subject_line: From physiotherapy to poetry: what being well means
email_body:
Dear Sue,

Your path from physiotherapist and acupuncturist to poet, novelist and essayist, and then a PhD asking how stories and poems can help us understand what being well means, is not one many writers have walked. Out of Shape seems to sit right at that crossing of medicine and the humanities.

I would love to ask what the clinic taught you about language, and what the Katherine Mansfield Menton Fellowship gave you as a Dunedin writer.
